title: Confidence intervals
summary: Estimate ± margin of error: building, interpreting and planning confidence intervals.
bookRef: Contrasted in ITILA ch. 37 (Bayesian Inference and Sampling Theory); see session 13
objectives: Build a confidence interval as point estimate ± z* × SE.
Interpret the confidence level correctly as a long-run capture rate.
Compute a margin of error and the sample size needed for a target margin.
Explain how sample size and confidence level change the width.

warmup.prompt: **Predict.** A poll reports 52% ± 3 points with 95% confidence. Which reading is correct?
options: The method used captures the true share in about 95% of polls like this
There is a 95% chance that 52% is exactly the true share
95% of voters are within 3 points of 52%
The true share is certainly between 49% and 55%
warmup.explain: The 95% describes the *method*: across many polls, about 95% of intervals built this way contain the true share. Hold on to that sentence; this session shows why it is the right one.

blocks.md:
## From a point to a range
A point estimate such as $\hat p = 0.56$ is almost never exactly right. A **confidence interval** gives a range of plausible values:

$$\text{point estimate} \pm \underbrace{z^* \times SE}_{\text{margin of error}}$$

$z^*$ sets the confidence level: it is the number of standard errors needed to capture the central part of a normal curve.

| Confidence | 90% | 95% | 99% |
|---|---|---|---|
| $z^*$ | 1.645 | 1.96 | 2.576 |

## A confidence interval for a proportion
$$\hat p \pm z^* \sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}}$$

**Conditions:** independent observations (a random sample) and the success-failure condition with $\hat p$: at least 10 successes and 10 failures.

blocks.title: A survey of 1,000 adults
steps: 560 of 1,000 randomly sampled adults support a policy: $\hat p = 0.56$. Successes 560 and failures 440 are both at least 10.
Conclusion: we are 95% confident that between 52.9% and 59.1% of all adults support the policy.

blocks.md: **Predict:** if you draw 40 intervals at 95% confidence, how many will miss the true $p$? Draw several batches. Then switch to 99%: what happens to the width, and to the number of misses?

**"There is a 95% probability that $p$ is in (0.529, 0.591)."** The true $p$ is a fixed number; it does not jump around. Before sampling, the *procedure* had a 95% chance of producing an interval that captures $p$. Afterwards, this particular interval either contains $p$ or it does not. That is why we say "95% **confident**".

## Width: confidence versus precision
- **Higher confidence → wider interval.** To be right more often you must cast a wider net.
- **Larger sample → narrower interval**, but only by $\sqrt{n}$: four times the data halves the width.

**Planning a study.** To get a margin of error of at most $m$ for a proportion, solve $m = z^*\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$ for $n$:
$$n \ge \frac{(z^*)^2\, p(1-p)}{m^2}$$
If you have no idea what $p$ is, use $p = 0.5$: it makes $p(1-p)$ as large as possible, so the sample is big enough whatever the truth. Always round **up**.

blocks.title: How big should the poll be?
steps: Target: margin of error at most 3 points (0.03) at 95% confidence, no prior guess for $p$.
Round up: sample at least 1,068 people. (That is why so many national polls use about 1,000-1,100 respondents.)

blocks.md:
## Intervals for a mean
For a mean with a large sample, the same recipe works: $\bar x \pm z^*\, s/\sqrt{n}$. With small samples, replace $z^*$ by a slightly larger $t^*$ from the **t-distribution**, which accounts for the extra uncertainty of estimating $\sigma$ by $s$ (book §7.1).

blocks.prompt: Why not always report 99.9% confidence intervals?
blocks.answer: Higher confidence makes the interval wider and less informative: '(10%, 90%)' is almost certainly right but useless. Confidence trades against precision; only more data buys both.

quiz.prompt: A 95% confidence interval for a proportion is (0.41, 0.47). Which interpretation is correct?
options: If we repeated the sampling many times, about 95% of intervals built this way would contain the true proportion
There is a 95% probability that the true proportion lies between 0.41 and 0.47
95% of the sample lies between 0.41 and 0.47
The sample proportion lies in this interval with probability 0.95
quiz.explain: The confidence level is a property of the method across repeated samples. The sample proportion (0.44) is always at the centre of its own interval.

quiz.prompt: The sample size goes from 100 to 400, at the same confidence level. The interval becomes:
quiz.explain: The width is proportional to $1/\sqrt{n}$, and $\sqrt{400/100} = 2$.

quiz.prompt: Using the same data, you switch from 95% to 99% confidence. The interval:
quiz.explain: $z^*$ grows from 1.96 to 2.576, so the margin of error grows. The centre $\hat p$ stays put.

cards.front: General form of a confidence interval?
cards.back: point estimate ± $z^* \times SE$; the second part is the margin of error.
$\hat p \pm z^* \sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$, if independence and success-failure (≥10 each) hold.
The method captures the true parameter in about 95% of repeated samples. A single computed interval either contains it or not.

cards.front: Sample size for margin of error $m$ (proportion)?
cards.back: $n \ge (z^*)^2 p(1-p)/m^2$; use $p = 0.5$ if unknown, and round up.

cards.front: What makes a confidence interval narrower?
cards.back: A larger sample (width ∝ $1/\sqrt{n}$) or a lower confidence level.
